content_voiceover: This slide covers the differential diagnosis for a bleeding tendency when both PT and aPTT come back normal, which is a classic board exam trap because normal coagulation screening doesn't rule out a bleeding disorder. Some cases of von Willebrand disease, especially type one, can present with normal PT and aPTT since the defect is often mild or primarily affects platelet adhesion rather than the intrinsic or extrinsic pathways strongly enough to prolong screening tests. Thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction is another cause, since platelet problems don't show up on PT or aPTT, which only measure the coagulation cascade, not primary hemostasis. Dysfibrinogenemia, an abnormality in fibrinogen function rather than quantity, is worked up with fibrinogen level, thrombin time, and reptilase time. Factor thirteen deficiency is a particularly important one to remember, because factor thirteen acts downstream of fibrin formation to cross link and stabilize the clot, so it's invisible to PT and aPTT entirely, and you need a specific clot stability test using urea solution to detect it. Alpha two antiplasmin deficiency causes excessive fibrinolysis and also won't prolong PT or aPTT. Finally, vascular or connective tissue abnormalities, like those seen in Ehlers Danlos syndrome, can cause bleeding purely from fragile vessel walls without any coagulation factor abnormality at all.
keypoints: Von Willebrand disease, especially type one, can have normal PT and aPTT
Thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction are not detected by PT or aPTT
Factor thirteen deficiency is invisible to PT and aPTT, use the urea clot stability test
Dysfibrinogenemia needs fibrinogen level, thrombin time, and reptilase time
Vascular or connective tissue disorders can cause bleeding with normal coagulation tests
keypoint_voiceover: Remember this list whenever you see a bleeding patient with reassuringly normal PT and aPTT. Think von Willebrand disease type one, platelet quantity or quality problems, dysfibrinogenemia, and especially factor thirteen deficiency, which requires a dedicated urea clot stability test since it acts after the clot has already formed. Also keep alpha two antiplasmin deficiency and vascular or connective tissue disorders on your differential.
